g.text: S[C] = [A1, X2, B3, D4]. Between two consecutive leavers

text.font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

g.text: of C, someone must have entered C (here X1, then B2).

text.font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

g.text: That entering move got an edge from the previous leaver,

text.font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

g.text: and its own robot's type-1 chain leads to the next leaver.

text.font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

g.text: So A1 reaches X2 and X2 reaches B3, and one edge B3 →

g.text: (b) Corner case: the latest candidate is the target's own robot

text.font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

g.text: Mini plan on vertices u, v, w, x: P leaves v at t = 1; Q enters v (Q1), leaves to w (Q2) and comes back

text.font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

g.text: (Q3). For Q3, S[v] = [P1, Q2] and the binary search lands on Q2, robot Q itself.

g.text: Why the latest candidate is enough (Theorem 3)

text.font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

g.text: Every move that leaves a vertex is ordered after every earlier move that left it, through the robots that entered in between. So a target only needs an edge from the most recent leaver;

text.font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

g.text: edges from older leavers (red, added by CP) are implied.
